meta.descriptionEn: In 1923 a single faint star on a photographic plate changed the size of the universe. Before that, most astronomers believed the Milky Way was everything, and the misty 'nebulae' were just clouds inside it. Then Edwin Hubble, working at Mount Wilson with the 100-inch Hooker telescope, found a special pulsating star in the Andromeda Nebula. What did that star tell him? Why did the great astronomers of the time refuse to believe it? And how did the same man later show that the universe is expanding? Follow the debate, the discovery, the mistakes and the surprising twists, from Henrietta Leavitt's early work to today's Hubble images of Andromeda. This is the story of the night the sky got bigger.
meta.descriptionUr: Ek chhota sa sitara, ek photographic plate aur poori kainat ka nazariya badal gaya. Pehle aksar astronomers samajhte thay ke Milky Way hi sab kuch hai aur 'nebulae' sirf badal hain. Phir Edwin Hubble ne Mount Wilson ki 100-inch Hooker telescope se Andromeda mein ek khaas pulsating sitara dhoonda. Us sitare ne kya bataya? Bade bade scientists ne kyun inkar kiya? Aur baad mein kainat ke phailne ka raaz kaise khula? Is documentary mein dekhein poori kahani, Urdu aur English mein, us raat ki jab aasman bada ho gaya.

articleEn: It is night on Mount Wilson in California. A large dome opens, and inside it the 100-inch Hooker telescope turns toward the sky. In front of it stands Edwin Hubble, studying the faint glow of the Andromeda Nebula on a glass plate. Between 1923 and 1924 he found a star in this nebula that was a Cepheid variable. It was a tiny mark, but it carried enormous meaning.

At that time, most astronomers believed the entire universe was just the Milky Way. Then one star changed that view. But what exactly did this single star prove? How can such a small star reveal the distance across the cosmos? And when Hubble announced his result, why did so many big names in astronomy stand against him? Above all, how big is the universe really?

The answer came through the work of a woman, an old debate, and many mistakes. On this journey we will look at the ancient history of Andromeda, understand the secret of Cepheid stars, and walk into the arena of the Great Debate. So let us begin the story whose first page was written on a photographic plate.

articleEn: In Hubble's time, most people believed the whole universe was the Milky Way. But the story of Andromeda is much older. Many faint objects were then called nebulae and were thought to be clouds of gas and dust. Several of them turned out to be real galaxies. Around 964 CE, the Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi described it in his Book of Fixed Stars as a small cloud or faint smudge. This was the first historical mention of Andromeda, and also the oldest known reference to any galaxy outside the Milky Way. Star charts of that era called it the Little Cloud.

In 1612 the German astronomer Simon Marius gave an early description of it using a telescope. John Flamsteed listed it as 33 Andromedae. In 1745 Pierre Louis Maupertuis suggested that this hazy mark might be an island universe. In 1755 the philosopher Immanuel Kant wrote that the Milky Way might be only one of many galaxies, and that oval-shaped nebulae could be such galaxies. His argument was that a disk like the Milky Way would look round from above and like an ellipsoid when seen at a slant. But at the time this was only a hypothesis.

In 1764 Charles Messier catalogued it as M31, though he mistakenly credited Marius as its discoverer, even though it can be seen with the naked eye. In 1785 William Herschel noticed a faint reddish tint at its center. He estimated it to be about 18,000 light-years away, which was wrong. In 1850 the Earl of Rosse drew its spiral structure. In 1864 William Huggins found that its spectrum differed from that of a gas nebula. It showed dark absorption lines over a continuum, which reveal chemical composition, and from this it was inferred that it contained stars.

In 1885 a new light appeared in Andromeda, called S Andromedae. It was taken for a nova, since the difference between novae and supernovae was not yet known. In 1888 Isaac Roberts took one of the first photographs of Andromeda. He regarded Andromeda and similar spiral nebulae as star systems in formation. Then in 1912 Vesto Slipher measured Andromeda's radial velocity using spectroscopy. At 300 km/s it was the largest velocity measured up to that time. So Andromeda was not just a faint cloud; it was also moving fast. But the question remained: how far away was it?

articleEn: Stars in the sky generally seem to shine with a steady light. But some seem to breathe, growing bright and then dim. These are called Cepheid variables. They pulsate radially, meaning both their diameter and temperature keep changing. On 10 September 1784, Edward Pigott found that Eta Aquilae was variable, the first known example of a classical Cepheid. A few months later John Goodricke found Delta Cephei to be variable, and the whole class is named after that star. By the end of the nineteenth century, several dozen such stars were known. But their greatest use had yet to appear.

Then in 1908 Henrietta Swan Leavitt studied thousands of variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds. A surprising relationship emerged. She discovered a strong, direct link between the luminosity of a classical Cepheid and its pulsation period. Leavitt published this in 1912. By measuring the period, one could learn the star's true brightness, and astronomers had a ruler.

Think of it this way. If you know a star's true luminosity and you also measure its apparent brightness from Earth, comparing the two gives the distance. It is like seeing a bulb far away at night when you already know its real power: the dimmer it looks, the farther away it is. But the ruler must first be calibrated. For this, the parallax distances of nearby Cepheids, such as RS Puppis and Polaris, are measured directly. Delta Cephei is also important for calibration. It is a member of a cluster, and its distance is known from precise parallax measurements by the Hubble Space Telescope, Hipparcos and Gaia.

But why does a Cepheid brighten and dim? The answer is the kappa mechanism, also called the Eddington valve, and helium plays the main role. Doubly ionized helium is more opaque than singly ionized helium, so it absorbs the star's heat and expands. As it expands it cools, becomes singly ionized and more transparent, and then gravity pulls it back in. The cycle repeats. The history is interesting too: in 1917 Arthur Stanley Eddington described the pulsation as a heat engine, and in 1953 S. A. Zhevakin suggested ionized helium as the likely valve.
So if a Cepheid could be found inside a hazy nebula, could it end the whole debate? The answer was coming soon.

articleEn: So who was Edwin Powell Hubble? He was born in 1889 in Marshfield, Missouri, and in 1900 his family moved to Wheaton, Illinois. At the University of Chicago he studied mathematics, astronomy and philosophy, and he received his Bachelor of Science degree by 1910. He then went to The Queen's College, Oxford, as a Rhodes Scholar. Instead of science he studied jurisprudence, because he had promised his father he would.

His father died in the winter of 1913, while Edwin was in England. The following summer he returned to look after his family. He had no heart for law. He taught Spanish, physics and mathematics at New Albany High School in Indiana and also coached the boys' basketball team. Since childhood his real interest had been astronomy, so after a year of teaching he went to Yerkes Observatory, where he received his Ph.D. in 1921. In 1917, when America declared war on Germany, Hubble finished his dissertation quickly and joined the Army. He became a major. His 86th Division went overseas but never fought in battle.

After the war Hubble studied astronomy for a year at the University of Cambridge. Then in 1919 George Ellery Hale offered him a staff position at Mount Wilson Observatory. Hubble stayed there until his death in 1953. Mount Wilson is a 5,710-foot peak in the San Gabriel Mountains near Pasadena. But why was the place so special? An inversion layer above Los Angeles traps warm air and smog, so the air here is the steadiest in North America.

The founder of the observatory was George Ellery Hale, who received funding from the Carnegie Institution in 1904. Hale had already built Yerkes's large telescope, and he now wanted an even bigger one. John D. Hooker gave 45,000 dollars for the mirror, and Andrew Carnegie provided the rest of the money. The mirror blank was cast in France by the Saint-Gobain factory. After great difficulties, the Hooker telescope saw first light on 2 November 1917. This giant 100-inch telescope was the largest in the world from 1917 to 1949, and its 100-ton weight was supported by mercury floats. This was the telescope Hubble would sit at. Could it unlock the secret of a faint patch of sky?

articleEn: So where did this debate begin? On 26 April 1920, at the U.S. National Museum in Washington, D.C., Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis faced each other. It is called the Shapley–Curtis Debate or the Great Debate. The topic was what spiral nebulae are and how large the universe is.

Shapley presented a Milky Way 300,000 light-years wide, with the Sun off to one side. He derived these estimates from Cepheids in globular clusters. His argument was that nebulae like Andromeda lie on the edge of the Milky Way. If they were separate galaxies, the distances would be so large that most astronomers would not accept them.

Curtis took the opposite position. His Milky Way was only 30,000 light-years wide, one tenth of Shapley's estimate. In his view Andromeda and other nebulae were small, separate galaxies. This idea is called island universes, a term from Immanuel Kant. Curtis offered evidence from novae. In 1917 he had seen a nova in Andromeda, found 11 more in older photographs, and they were on average 10 magnitudes fainter. From this Curtis derived a distance of 500,000 light-years. That is about five times too small by today's value, but it was a correct first estimate within a factor of ten.

He also mentioned dark lanes in Andromeda that looked like the Milky Way's dust clouds, and the large radial velocities of nebulae. Another point was the Zone of Avoidance. According to Curtis, the Milky Way's dust blocks our view, which is why spiral nebulae are not seen along the plane.

Interestingly, no transcript of that night exists. The debate has been pieced together from Shapley's annotated script, Curtis's slides and letters from both. In May 1921 their arguments were published as separate technical papers under the title The Scale of the Universe. Each read the other's paper and improved his reply.

Shapley relied on the work of Adriaan van Maanen, who claimed that the Pinwheel Galaxy had been seen rotating. If it were truly a separate galaxy, its speed in such a short time would exceed the speed of light, which would violate physics. Shapley also raised the nova of 1885, which for a while outshone the whole Andromeda Nebula. Such energy seemed impossible in a separate galaxy.

Curtis replied that van Maanen's measurements were too small to be trusted. The 1885 nova was an outlier, and two classes of novae were possible. Later it turned out that van Maanen's observations were wrong, and that the 1885 nova was actually a supernova, which can briefly outshine an entire galaxy. So who won that night? The verdict was still to come. Someone had to bring a sign from the sky that no one could reject.

articleEn: Now it was Hubble's turn. When he arrived at Mount Wilson the Hooker telescope was complete, and the common view then was that the whole universe was just the Milky Way. Hubble searched for Cepheid variables with the Hooker. By comparing their apparent and true brightness, distance could be calculated. This was Leavitt's ruler. He found Cepheids in several nebulae, including the Andromeda Nebula and the Triangulum Nebula. The result was clear: these nebulae were much too far away to be part of the Milky Way. They were not nebulae but whole galaxies, many millions of light-years from the Milky Way. Today they are no longer called nebulae.

Here the dates deserve attention, because sources do not agree. According to a Mount Wilson article, Hubble found the first Cepheid in Andromeda in 1923. Another source says Edwin Hubble first identified extragalactic Cepheid variables on Andromeda photographs in 1925 and ended the debate. Hubble's biography and the article on Cepheids say 1924. So it is better to see this story in stages rather than as a single day.

On 23 November 1924 Hubble's results appeared in the New York Times. Then on 1 January 1925 he presented them to astronomers at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society. But the Andromeda results were formally published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal only in 1929. In other words: first the newspaper, then the meeting, and finally the journal.

The opposition was considerable. Many big names in astronomy, including Harvard's Harlow Shapley, were against Hubble's view, and some mocked his results. Hubble published them anyway. For this work he received the American Association Prize, along with 500 dollars from Burton E. Livingston.

The idea was not new. In 1755 Immanuel Kant had hypothesized that the Milky Way is one of many galaxies, and Hubble's Cepheids gave it a foundation. Remember another name: in 1922 Ernst Öpik derived a distance from the velocities of stars in Andromeda and placed it far outside the Milky Way, at about 450 kpc.

So what was the final verdict? On the basic question Heber Curtis was proved right: spirals like Andromeda are separate galaxies. But Shapley was right on many points too. He put the Sun in the outer part of the galaxy, whereas in Curtis's model the Sun was near the center. The true size of the Milky Way came out between the two estimates, and van Maanen's observations proved wrong. The Pinwheel Galaxy does not appear to rotate on a human timescale.

Hubble also sorted galaxies into groups by their shape, which is called the Hubble sequence. That system is still the most widely used today. We now know that the Milky Way is one galaxy, and that the observable universe may hold from 200 billion to 2 trillion galaxies or more. But how far away is Andromeda exactly? And was there a hidden error in Hubble's Cepheids? The answer comes in the next part.

articleEn: So was there really a hidden error in Hubble's Cepheids? Yes there was, and its story is as interesting as the discovery itself. In the 1940s Walter Baade noticed that Cepheids are in fact of two kinds: classical Cepheids and type II Cepheids. Type II Cepheids are older and fainter stars. Their light is on average about 1.5 magnitudes less than classical Cepheids, and the two follow different period-luminosity relations. This doubled the distance to Andromeda, and the rest of the extragalactic scale grew too. Sources disagree on the date: some say the 1940s, others 1953.

Hubble's own estimates also turned out too small. Today we know all his distances were too low, by up to about a factor of 7. The reasons included confusing the two kinds of Cepheids and mistaking bright gas clouds for bright stars.

Hubble estimated distances for 24 extra-galactic nebulae and compared them with radial velocities known from their redshifts. The redshift measurements were by Vesto Slipher and Milton Humason. The result was that the farther a galaxy is, the faster it appears to move away from us. This became known as Hubble's law. Based on 46 galaxies, the Hubble constant came out as 500 km/s/Mpc, far higher than today's values. Today the distance ladder method gives about 74 and the CMB method about 68 km/s/Mpc. The difference came from errors in distance calibration.

But the question remained: what causes the redshift? Two years earlier, in 1927, Georges Lemaître had predicted this very relationship on the basis of general relativity. In 2011 Nature reported claims that Hubble might have played a part in getting some passages removed from the 1931 English translation, though historians were doubtful. Then in November 2011 Mario Livio reported in Nature that a letter had been found in Lemaître's archive, according to which Lemaître himself made the omission.

Hubble himself was cautious about explaining the relationship. In a 1931 letter he and Humason spoke of 'apparent' velocities and left the interpretation to other experts. According to Allan Sandage, Hubble to the end preferred, or at least kept open, a model without real expansion. In December 1941 he reported that the results of a six-year survey did not support the expanding universe theory.

In 1917 Einstein's equations indicated that the universe was either expanding or contracting. He added the cosmological constant, which was called a 'fudge factor'. Seeing Hubble's redshifts, Einstein came to understand that the expansion was real. Later he called changing his equations the biggest mistake of his life. In 1931 Einstein visited Mount Wilson and met Hubble, and there he announced that the visit had changed his mind.
Finally, there is one more problem tied to Cepheids. Values of the Hubble constant derived from classical Cepheids are still reported to lie between 60 and 80 km/s/Mpc.

articleEn: Now to Andromeda today. The question is the same one Hubble faced: how far away is this galaxy? At least four different techniques have now been used. In 2003, infrared surface brightness fluctuations gave 2.57 million light-years, and the 2004 Cepheid method gave 2.51 million. In 2005 an eclipsing binary was found in Andromeda, giving 2.52 million light-years. The same year the TRGB method gave 2.56 million. Their average is about 2.54 million light-years. That different methods agree so closely increases confidence in the measurement.

Structurally, Andromeda is a barred spiral galaxy. Its classification from visible light was different, but infrared data revealed the bar. Its D25 diameter is about 152,000 light-years, making it the largest galaxy in the Local Group in terms of extent.

Its mass is still debated. Older estimates held Andromeda to be heavier than the Milky Way, but 2018 radio results showed the two as roughly equal. At its center sits the supermassive black hole M31*. A 2005 measurement put its mass between 110 and 230 million solar masses. About 460 globular clusters are attached to Andromeda. The most massive is Mayall II, which is brighter than any other known globular cluster in the Local Group. It also has smaller companions. More than 20 dwarf galaxies are known, and the most famous and easily seen are M32 and M110.

In 2025 NASA released a very large Hubble mosaic. It was built from about 600 overlapping fields, drawn from 10 years of observations. In it Hubble sees about 200 million individual stars that are hotter than the Sun. Even so, this is only a fraction of the total stellar population.

Now the most famous question: the collision of Andromeda and the Milky Way. Andromeda is approaching us at about 110 km/s. A collision within 4 billion years was once predicted. But after Gaia found a larger sideways velocity, the chance of a merger came out much lower. Another source, however, puts the chance of a collision within the next 10 billion years at about 50 percent. So the sources do not agree.
And you can see it yourself. Its apparent magnitude is 3.44, and on new moon nights it can be seen with the naked eye.

articleEn: So what did this one star change? In 1924 Hubble proved that Andromeda is not a nebula inside the Milky Way but a separate galaxy. After that the universe was no longer a place with a single galaxy. Today it is estimated that the observable universe may hold 200 billion to 2 trillion galaxies or more.

Hubble received many honors in his lifetime: the Newcomb Cleveland Prize in 1924, the Bruce Medal in 1938, the Franklin Medal in 1939, and the Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society in 1940. But one thing he did not have: a Nobel Prize. In those days the Nobel Prize in Physics did not include astronomy. Hubble spent a large part of the later years of his career trying to get astronomy accepted as part of physics, so that astronomers too could be recognized. That campaign did not succeed in his lifetime. But right after his death the Nobel Committee decided that astronomical work was also worthy of the physics prize. His name lives on today through the Hubble Space Telescope, and a model of that telescope is prominently displayed in his hometown of Marshfield, Missouri.

Now for the lessons. The first is that evidence wins. Shapley's Milky Way was a very big estimate and Curtis's a very small one, and the real size came out between the two. The second: in every debate, both sides can be partly right. Curtis was right on the question of galaxies, but Shapley was right about the Sun's position. The third: being wrong is nothing to be ashamed of. Hubble's distances were too small, van Maanen's rotation was wrong, and even Einstein called changing his equations a mistake.

Some questions remain open today. The first is the correct value of the Hubble constant, which is still debated. The second is the mass of Andromeda. Some studies put it equal to the Milky Way, but a 2019 calculation puts it at half the Milky Way. The third is the collision. Will Andromeda and the Milky Way really merge? The fate of the Solar System is currently unknown.
And one question was Hubble's own. To the end he kept open the possibility that redshift might be some unknown natural principle rather than real expansion.

shorts.roman: Kya poori kainat sirf hamari Milky Way hai? 26 April 1920 ko Washington, D.C. ke U.S. National Museum mein do astronomers aamne samne aaye. Un ka kehna tha ke Andromeda jaise nebulae isi Milky Way ke kinare par hain. Curtis ka mauqif ulta tha. Un ki Milky Way sirf 30,000 light-years chauri thi, yani daswan hissa. Aur un ke mutabiq yeh nebulae alag galaxies thin. Is debate ka koi transcript maujood nahin. To aakhir kaun sahi nikla? Faisla ek sitaray ne kiya. Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

shorts.text: کیا Hubble کے Cepheids میں ایک چھپی ہوئی غلطی تھی؟ جی ہاں، تھی۔ 1940s میں Walter Baade نے دیکھا کہ Cepheids دو قسم کے ہیں۔ ایک classical Cepheids، اور دوسرے type II Cepheids۔ Type II پرانے ستارے ہیں، اور اوسطاً تقریباً 1.5 magnitudes کم روشن۔ اس سے Andromeda کا فاصلہ دگنا ہو گیا۔ یہاں sources میں اختلاف ہے: کہیں یہ دریافت 1940s میں بتائی گئی ہے، اور کہیں 1953 میں۔ آج معلوم ہے کہ Hubble کے سارے distances حقیقت سے کم تھے، کبھی تقریباً 7 گنا تک۔ اس کا Hubble constant 500 نکلا، جبکہ آج 74 یا 68 مانا جاتا ہے۔ تو کیا اس غلطی سے اس کی دریافت ختم ہو گئی؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya Hubble ke Cepheids mein ek chhupi hui ghalti thi? Ji haan, thi. 1940s mein Walter Baade ne dekha ke Cepheids do qism ke hain. Ek classical Cepheids, aur doosray type II Cepheids. Type II purane sitaray hain, aur ausatan taqriban 1.5 magnitudes kam roshan. Is se Andromeda ka fasla dugna ho gaya. Yahan sources mein ikhtilaf hai: kahin yeh daryaft 1940s mein batai gai hai, aur kahin 1953 mein. Aaj maloom hai ke Hubble ke saray distances haqeeqat se kam thay, kabhi taqriban 7 guna tak. Is ka Hubble constant 500 nikla, jabke aaj 74 ya 68 mana jata hai. To kya is ghalti se is ki daryaft khatam ho gai? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

Walter Baade found that Cepheid stars come in two types, which doubled the distance to Andromeda.
Hubble's own distances were too small, yet his discovery of the expanding universe still stands.
